shared_context.patient: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below: Serum: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

atoms.1: Morning stiffness and improvement with activity are characteristic symptoms of inflammatory back pain.
atoms.2: Limited spinal mobility is suggestive of enthesitis.
atoms.3: Tenderness at tendon insertion sites is suggestive of enthesitis.
atoms.4: Enthesitis is commonly seen in spondyloarthropathies.
atoms.5: Elevated ESR is indicative of an inflammatory process.
atoms.6: Elevated CRP is indicative of an inflammatory process.
atoms.7: The combination of chronic lower back pain, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, enthesitis, and elevated inflammatory markers is highly suggestive of Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS).
atoms.8: Ankylosing Spondylitis typically presents with chronic back pain that improves with exercise.
atoms.9: Ankylosing Spondylitis is associated with enthesitis.
atoms.10: Ankylosing Spondylitis is associated with elevated inflammatory markers.
atoms.11: Imaging studies are crucial to confirm the diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis.
atoms.12: Radiographs (X-rays) are typically the initial imaging modality to look for changes in the sacroiliac joints.
atoms.13: Plain radiographs may not detect early changes in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
atoms.14: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than X-rays.
atoms.15: MRI can detect early inflammatory changes such as bone marrow edema.
atoms.16: Bone marrow edema is not visible on X-rays.
atoms.17: MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting early sacroiliitis in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
atoms.18: MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting other inflammatory changes in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
atoms.19: The most accurate test for diagnosing this patient's condition is Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).

Ankylosing Spondylitis typically presents with chronic back pain that improves with exercise.
Ankylosing Spondylitis is associated with enthesitis.
Ankylosing Spondylitis is associated with elevated inflammatory markers.
Imaging studies are crucial to confirm the diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis.
